author: Supreme Court of the United States (opinion of the Court by Stewart, J.; concurrences by Douglas, Harlan and White, JJ.; dissent by Black, J.)

relevant_locations: Syllabus (docket No. 35; argued Oct 17, 1967; decided Dec 18, 1967; vote 7-1)

Opinion of the Court (Stewart, J.) — facts, 'protects people, not places', 'knowingly exposes to the public' passage, phone-booth/'shuts the door...pays the toll' passage, 'search and seizure' holding, warrant/prior-judicial-authorization requirement, overruling of Olmstead and Goldman trespass doctrine
Concurring opinion (Harlan, J.) — two-part 'actual (subjective) expectation of privacy ... society is prepared to recognize as reasonable' test
Dissenting opinion (Black, J.) — Fourth Amendment protects tangible things; eavesdropping is not a search or seizure

notes: Primary opinion for 389 U.S. 347. Durable content hash of the LII canonical text page captured 2026-07-04. Confirms: 7-1; Stewart majority; Harlan, White and Douglas (joined by Brennan) concurring; Black dissenting; Marshall took no part. FBI attached an electronic listening-and-recording device to the OUTSIDE of a public telephone booth in Los Angeles to record Katz transmitting wagering information by telephone across state lines (to Miami and Boston) in violation of 18 U.S.C. 1084; no physical penetration/trespass; held a 'search and seizure'; unconstitutional because conducted without prior approval of a judge or magistrate despite probable cause and restraint; the 'trespass' doctrine of Olmstead and Goldman no longer controlling. Decided Dec 18, 1967.
